content: Proline is an α-amino acid and one of the twenty amino acids encoded by DNA. Its codons are CCU, CCC, CCA, and CCG. It is classified as a non-essential amino acid, meaning that humans can synthesize it endogenously. Proline is unique among the proteinogenic amino acids because its α-amino group is secondary, forming a cyclic structure. Biosynthesis Proline is biosynthetically derived from the amino acid L-glutamate. The immediate precursor in this pathway is the imino acid (S)-Δ¹-pyrroline-5-carboxylate (P5C). The enzymes involved in its biosynthesis include: Glutamate kinase: This enzyme is ATP-dependent. Glutamate dehydrogenase: This enzyme requires NADH or NADPH as cofactors. Pyrroline-5-carboxylate reductase: This enzyme also requires NADH or NADPH. Structural Properties Proline’s side chain forms a distinctive cyclic structure, which locks its φ (phi) backbone dihedral angle at approximately -75°. This unique conformation imparts exceptional rigidity compared to other amino acids. As a result, proline loses less conformational entropy during protein folding, which may explain its higher prevalence in proteins of thermophilic organisms. Proline acts as a structural disruptor in the middle of regular secondary structure elements such as α-helices and β-sheets. However, it is frequently found as the first residue of an α-helix and in the edge strands of β-sheets. Proline is also commonly located in turns, which may explain why it is often solvent-exposed despite having a completely aliphatic side chain. Due to the absence of a hydrogen atom on its amide group, proline cannot act as a hydrogen bond donor and can only function as a hydrogen bond acceptor. Multiple proline residues or hydroxyproline residues in sequence can form a polyproline helix, which is the predominant secondary structure in collagen. Hydroxylation of proline by the enzyme prolyl hydroxylase (or the addition of other electron-withdrawing substituents like fluorine) significantly increases the conformational stability of collagen. This hydroxylation process is critical for maintaining the structural integrity of connective tissues in higher organisms. Mutations in prolyl hydroxylase or a deficiency in the necessary cofactor ascorbate (vitamin C) can impair this process. Sequences of proline and 2-aminoisobutyric acid (Aib) can also form helical turn structures. In 2006, researchers at Arizona State University discovered that solutions of titanium dioxide (TiO₂) illuminated with ultraviolet radiation can serve as highly cost-effective and accurate protein cleavage catalysts. The TiO₂ catalyst preferentially and rapidly cleaves proteins at sites where proline is present, while taking significantly longer to degrade proteins from their endpoints. Cis-Trans Isomerization Peptide bonds involving proline and other N-substituted amino acids (e.g., sarcosine) can adopt both cis and trans isomers. Under unstrained conditions, approximately 9% of these bonds exist in the cis configuration. This is primarily because the amide hydrogen in the trans isomer offers less steric repulsion to the preceding Cα atom compared to the following Cα atom in the cis isomer. In contrast, the cis and trans isomers of the X-Pro peptide bond (where X is any amino acid) both experience steric clashes with neighboring substitutions, making them nearly equally energetically unfavorable. Consequently, the fraction of X-Pro peptide bonds in the cis isomer under unstrained conditions ranges from 10-40%, depending slightly on the preceding amino acid. Aromatic residues tend to favor the cis isomer slightly. From a kinetic perspective, cis-trans proline isomerization is a slow process that can hinder protein folding by trapping one or more proline residues in the non-native isomer, especially when the native protein requires the cis isomer. This is because proline residues are exclusively synthesized in the ribosome as the trans isomer. All organisms possess prolyl isomerase enzymes to catalyze this isomerization, and some bacteria have specialized prolyl isomerases associated with the ribosome. However, not all proline residues are essential for folding, and protein folding may proceed at a normal rate despite the presence of non-native conformers of many X-Pro peptide bonds. Usage Proline and its derivatives are frequently used as asymmetric catalysts in organic reactions. Notable examples include the CBS reduction and proline-catalyzed aldol condensation. L-proline is also an ingredient in certain energy drinks, such as Sobe Power Fruit Punch. Proline has a sweet flavor with a distinct aftertaste.
